hints: Think about which type of chloride fizzes violently with cold water, which needs warming with NaOH, and which does not hydrolyse at all.
Focus on the carbon attached to Cl. How electron deficient is it, and how strong is the C-Cl bond in each case?
Link the C=O group, the alkyl group inductive effect, and the benzene delocalised system to bond strength and attack by water.
walkthrough:
Picture what hydrolysis needs**
Imagine a water molecule acting as a nucleophile, looking for a slightly positive carbon to attack and trying to break a $\text{C-Cl}$ bond. The faster this happens, the more electron deficient the carbon is and the weaker the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is. That is your comparison tool for all three types.

See why acyl chlorides are fastest**
Look at $\text{R-C(=O)-Cl}$. The carbon is joined to oxygen as well as chlorine, two very electronegative atoms pulling electrons away. So that carbon carries a large $\delta+$ charge and the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is weakened and highly polar. Water attacks instantly, even in cold water.

See why aryl chlorides do not react**
Now look at chlorobenzene. The lone pair in a p-orbital on $\text{Cl}$ overlaps with the delocalised $\pi$ system of the ring. This gives the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond partial double bond character, making it much shorter and stronger. Water cannot break it, so no hydrolysis occurs even on boiling with NaOH.

Place alkyl chlorides in the middle**
For $\text{R-Cl}$, the carbon is attached to only one electronegative atom. The alkyl group pushes electrons toward carbon by the positive inductive effect, reducing the $\delta+$ on carbon and strengthening the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond compared to an acyl chloride. Hydrolysis is therefore slower than acyl chlorides but still possible, unlike aryl chlorides.

Final answer: acyl chlorides (fastest) > alkyl chlorides > aryl chlorides (slowest).
Acyl chloride C-Cl is weakest as C is attached to two electronegative atoms (O and Cl) making C very $\delta+$, easily attacked by water.
Aryl chloride C-Cl has partial double bond character as Cl lone pair delocalises into benzene $\pi$ system, so bond is stronger and no hydrolysis.

hints: Count the hydrolysable groups in remifentanil. Look for $\text{COOCH}_3$ ester groups and the $\text{N-C=O}$ amide group.
Recall that acidic ester hydrolysis gives carboxylic acid plus alcohol, while acidic amide hydrolysis gives carboxylic acid plus ammonium salt.
The two ester groups both release the same alcohol, so identify that small alcohol and the two larger carboxylic acid fragments.
walkthrough:
Spot the three breakable links**
Work around the structure. On the left you have $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)OCH}_3$, a methyl ester. On the top right you have $\text{-C(COOCH}_3\text{)-}$, a second methyl ester. At the bottom right you have $\text{-N(Ph)-C(=O)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, an amide (a tertiary amide with phenyl and piperidine groups on N). All three hydrolyse in hot aqueous acid.

Hydrolyse the esters to acid plus alcohol**
Remember $\text{RCOOR' + H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCOOH + R'OH}$ in acid. Both esters are methyl esters, so both release $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. The left side becomes $\text{-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ still attached to the piperidine N. The top right becomes $\text{-C(COOH)-}$ still attached to the piperidine C-4.

Hydrolyse the amide to acid plus amine**
Remember $\text{RCONR'R'' + H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCOOH + HNR'R''}$ with protonation in acid. Here $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)-N(Ph)-}$ breaks to give $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ (propanoic acid) plus the free secondary amine $\text{-NHPh}$ attached to C-4 of the piperidine. In acid this amine and the piperidine N are protonated to ammonium salts, which is allowed.

Collect the three distinct organics**
Because methanol is formed twice it counts once. So you end with: small molecule 1, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$; small molecule 2, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$; large molecule 3, the piperidine ring bearing $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ on the ring N and bearing $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{NHPh}$ on C-4.

Final answer: Product 1: propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ from amide hydrolysis.
Product 2: methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ from both methyl esters.
Product 3: piperidine dicarboxylic acid derivative: N-(2-carboxyethyl) substituted piperidine with $\text{C(COOH)(NHPh)}$ at C-4, i.e. $\text{HOOCCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-N(C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{)-C(COOH)(NHPh)}$, amines protonated in acid allowed.

hints: Use the formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$ plus $\text{CO}_2$ evolution with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ to confirm a carboxylic acid, then match the 6H doublet plus 1H multiplet plus 2H doublet pattern to a branched chain.
walkthrough:
Let chemistry and NMR point to the skeleton**
Fizzing with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ tells you $\text{Y}$ is a carboxylic acid, so one carbon is $\text{COOH}$. That leaves $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9$. The spectrum in $\text{D}_2\text{O}$ shows no $\text{COOH}$ proton because it exchanges away. The huge doublet integrating to 6H at about 0.9 ppm is classic for two identical $\text{CH}_3$ groups next to one $\text{CH}$, the 1H multiplet is that $\text{CH}$, and the 2H doublet near 2.2 ppm is $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$. Join them as $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH-CH}_2\text{-COOH}$.

hints: Match each $\delta$ value to the groups in $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{COOH}$, remembering $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$ is most deshielded near 2.2 ppm.
Apply the n+1 rule: count neighbouring protons on adjacent carbons to predict doublet for $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2$ and multiplet for $\text{CH}$.
Use peak heights and the total of 9 C-bound protons to assign 6H to the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups, 1H to $\text{CH}$, and 2H to $\text{CH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Assign the 0.95 ppm tall doublet**
The tallest peak near 0.9 ppm is in the alkane region. In $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CH-}$ the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are equivalent, giving 6 protons. Each $\text{CH}_3$ sees one proton on the neighbouring $\text{CH}$, so n+1 = 2, a doublet. So environment: alkane $\text{CH}_3$, splitting: doublet, number: 6.

Assign the 1.90 ppm small multiplet**
The small complex signal near 1.9 ppm is the lone $\text{CH}$ proton. It is alkane $\text{CH}$ coupled to 6 protons on two $\text{CH}_3$ groups plus 2 protons on $\text{CH}_2$, giving many lines, a multiplet. So environment: alkane $\text{CH}$, splitting: multiplet, number: 1.

Assign the 2.20 ppm doublet**
The peak near 2.2 ppm is deshielded by the adjacent $\text{C=O}$, characteristic of $\text{R-CH}_2\text{-C(=O)OH}$. This $\text{CH}_2$ sees one proton on the neighbouring $\text{CH}$, so n+1 = 2, a doublet, integrating to 2H. So environment: alkyl $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$ / $\text{COOH}$, splitting: doublet, number: 2.

Final answer: $\delta$ 0.95: alkane $\text{CH}_3$, doublet, 6H.
$\delta$ 1.90: alkane $\text{CH}$, multiplet, 1H.
$\delta$ 2.20: $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$ / $\text{COOH}$, doublet, 2H.
